title: Agent Archivist control trust record envelope (archivist.control/v1)
description: The shared, versioned conventions every control trust record reuses (plan Section 5 control-plane boundary; docs/notes/control-trust-schemas.md). Control records are the tenant-authority-signed objects below `tenants/<tenant>/v1/control/` (plan Section 7.5): the linked-client and revocation records shipped alongside this file, and the receipt-key, delegation, and authority-rotation record types the control-plane boundary names, each arriving as its own schema composed from this document. This file is a conventions registry and shared member library, not an instance schema — the standing `ingest-identifiers.json` has in the wire family: no control object validates against it alone, and every record-type schema is the complete, closed, flat object (wrapper members from `wrapper.members` below plus the type's payload members, side by side, `additionalProperties: false`). The wrapper is deliberately not a nested envelope-with-record shape: the receipt-key certificate inside `ingest-receipt.json` is already a flat authority-signed control record, and that definition is consumed by this family, not duplicated (docs/notes/wire-schemas.md, open questions).

x-archivist.publicMaterialOnly: no member of any control record carries private-key material: every key-bearing member is a public half under a common shape, and the closed shape leaves no undeclared member for anything else to ride in (SEC-006). tools/check-control-schemas.py rejects private/secret/seed member names outright so the property is machine-checked, not aspirational
x-archivist.authorityChain: every control record is signed by the tenant authority: `authority_key_id` names the signing key and `authority_signature` carries the signature (construction `control-record-v1` below). In v1 the named key is the tenant authority root the client pinned during linking (ID-009); when the authority itself rotates, an authority-rotation record type chains successor keys to predecessor ones, and `authority_key_id` then names the signing authority record's key — the certificate's authority-resolution rule, applied family-wide. Verification always starts at the pinned root and walks forward; it never trusts a key because a record asserts it

writeClasses.immutable: written once at a record-type-derived key; the ControlAdminStore rejects an overwrite outright unless the bytes are the identical record (plan Section 5: it 'rejects overwrite of an incompatible immutable record'), so a lost-response retry of the same administrative write is an idempotent repair and nothing else can displace the object. No pointer is protected, so the signed epoch is not a wrapper requirement for this class — a type carries it only when the epoch is part of the record's identity (the revocation object key names the revoked epoch, and the shipped revocation record is the type that does)
writeClasses.current-pointer: one object per subject at a fixed key, holding the current state; a replacement is accepted only when its signed `authorization_epoch` strictly increases — equal or lower is a stale write and is rejected (plan Section 5). The signature covers the epoch, so replaying an older record cannot displace a newer pointer without the authority key; rollback is therefore impossible by construction, the same property the plan pins for derived-policy pointers (publish another higher-epoch record, never repoint to an older one)

trustRecordCacheTtlSeconds.appliesTo: every control record an ingestion replica loads while authenticating an uploader (the linked-client and revocation records shipped; delegation, receipt-key, and authority-rotation records when they ship)
trustRecordCacheTtlSeconds.crossRef: schemas/v1/control-client.json pins this value as x-archivist.trustRecordCacheTtlSeconds; schemas/v1/control-revocation.json pins it as x-archivist.revocationPropagationBoundSeconds; tools/check-control-schemas.py proves all three agree
trustRecordCacheTtlSeconds.description: The upper bound on how long a reader may serve a cached control record before re-reading the store (plan Section 5: trust records cache for at most 60 seconds; EC-09: a registry outage permits using an unexpired cached record for at most 60 seconds, then readiness comes off with a retryable 503 and no storage writes). Because a revocation takes effect through the reader's view of control state, this constant is also the maximum revocation propagation delay — the same number re-expressed where the revocation record needs it, never a second value.

authorizationWindowSeconds.appliesTo: the fresh-per-attempt authorization timestamp in the ingest attempt signature (schemas/v1/ingest-request.json)
authorizationWindowSeconds.crossRef: schemas/v1/ingest-request.json pins this value as x-archivist.authorizationWindowSeconds; tools/check-control-schemas.py proves the two agree
authorizationWindowSeconds.description: How long a fresh-per-attempt authorization proof stays valid (plan Section 5: request authorization is fresh per upload attempt and valid for five minutes; Section 7.2). A retry outside the window mints fresh authorization without changing occurrence or attestation identity, because attempt state never enters the immutable envelope. Registered here, beside the cache TTL, because the two bound the same exposure from opposite ends: revocation kills the epoch, this window kills the proof, and neither outlives its bound plus the skew allowance below.

clockSkewAllowanceSeconds.appliesTo: the age comparison at attempt verification: a timestamp within the authorization window is accepted with this much clock-skew tolerance in either direction
clockSkewAllowanceSeconds.crossRef: schemas/v1/ingest-request.json pins this value as x-archivist.clockSkewAllowanceSeconds; tools/check-control-schemas.py proves the two agree
clockSkewAllowanceSeconds.description: Clock-skew tolerance applied when checking the attempt timestamp against the authorization window (plan Section 5: valid for five minutes with at most five minutes of clock skew). Client and server clocks are not synchronized; the allowance keeps a legitimately fresh proof from failing on skew alone. It is named separately from the window rather than folded into it, because it protects a different clock — the verifier's, not the signer's — and the plan pins them as two five-minute values that must not silently become one ten-minute window.

signatures.key: the tenant authority key named by `authority_key_id` — the pinned root in v1, or an authority record's key once authority rotation exists (ID-009)
covered: canonical record bytes minus the `authority_signature` member
signatures.description: Ed25519 over the RFC 8785 canonicalization of the complete record object with the `authority_signature` member removed — exactly the receipt-key-v1 shape (schemas/v1/ingest-identifiers.json), reused deliberately so one verifier core walks both families. Domain separation under one authority key comes from the member sets: every control record's signed bytes contain the `schema` namespace member and no bare certificate's do, so the two signed byte ranges stay structurally distinct.

recordTypes.description: The linked-client record (plan Section 7.5 `tenants/<tenant>/v1/control/clients/<client>.json`): client identity, Ed25519 public key, base scopes, and the current authorization epoch (ID-003).

The revocation record (plan Section 7.5 `tenants/<tenant>/v1/control/revocations/<client>/<epoch>.json`): the append-only, epoch-addressed revocation of one client's authorization at one epoch (plan Section 5; ID-006), written together with a strictly higher-epoch linked-client pointer that is what actually fails stale-epoch attempts closed. `keyMembers` names the members the store derives the object key from — for this type the epoch is identity, not a pointer guard.

schema-namespace.description: The control trust namespace, expressed the way the `archivist.error/v1` and `archivist.cli-output/v1` families express theirs: one namespace member, present in every record, never implied by context, so a reader knows which contract it is reading before it looks at anything else. The trailing `v1` is the family's only version axis — there is no numeric twin beside it, and a v2 is a new namespace string, never a second field. Security-bearing: an unknown namespace fails closed; a trust record a reader cannot interpret is a verification failure, never a best-effort parse.

record-type.description: Which control record type the object is (plan Section 5: client, delegation, rotation, revocation, and receipt-verification-key records all live under the control prefix). Closed, and appended to only by the change that ships the new type's schema and its readers: v1 ships `linked-client` and `revocation`; receipt-key, delegation, and authority-rotation tokens arrive with their record types and old readers fail closed on them until upgraded — the plan Section 7.1 rule that unknown security-bearing values are never guessed. Each record-type schema pins this member to a const of its own token, so a record of one type can never validate as the other. Security-bearing.

record-kind.description: The write class (plan Section 5): `immutable` records are written once at a derived key with incompatible overwrites rejected; `current-pointer` records hold the current state of one subject and a replacement is valid only when its signed epoch increases (see `writeClasses`). The member must equal the write class registered for `record_type` in this schema's `recordTypes` registry — a cross-field check the ControlAdminStore makes before any write and any reader can re-make (VAL-002-style, not schema syntax). Security-bearing: the write rule is an authorization decision, so an unknown value fails closed.

authorization-epoch.description: The signed monotonic authorization epoch (plan Section 5: a current-pointer replacement is permitted only when its signed epoch increases; plan Phase 3: monotonic authorization epochs). Required on every current-pointer record; an immutable record type carries it only when the epoch is part of its identity (the revocation object key names the revoked epoch, and the shipped revocation record requires it as the identity member that equals that key segment). The authority signature covers it, so a stale record cannot displace a newer pointer and a revocation cannot be re-dated. Monotonic per client across every record that carries one: the linked-client pointer's epoch only increases, and each revocation record permanently fixes the epoch it revokes, so a client's authorization history is a strictly ascending sequence that no later write reorders — which is why revocation can be append-only. The maximum is the 18-digit canonical decimal the revocation object key can carry — the bound is held in lockstep with that grammar rather than at the raw u63 ceiling, and sits far above any real epoch count. On the wire, an attempt's authorization epoch must equal the current linked-client record's epoch: stale-epoch attempts fail closed (plan Phase 3 exit gate), and the receipt records which epoch actually authorized the commit.

client-object-key.description: Server-derived linked-client record key (plan Section 7.5): tenant, the fixed v1 control prefix, and the validated client UUID. One object per linked client — the current-pointer home whose replacement requires a strictly higher signed epoch. The tenant segment must equal the record's `tenant_id` and the client segment its `client_id` (VAL-002 cross-field checks at the store and at any reader; ID-008: keys are derived from validated fields, never chosen by a writer).

revocation-object-key.description: Server-derived revocation record key (plan Section 7.5): tenant, the revoked client, and the revoked authorization epoch in canonical decimal without leading zeros. One immutable object per (client, epoch) — the epoch addressing that makes revocation append-only, since a new revocation can only be a new epoch and no write ever removes or rewrites an old one. The tenant segment must equal the record's `tenant_id`, the client segment its `client_id`, and the epoch segment its signed `authorization_epoch` (VAL-002 cross-field checks at the store and at any reader; ID-008: keys are derived from validated fields, never chosen by a writer). The epoch grammar `[1-9][0-9]{0,17}` and the `authorization-epoch` maximum are held in lockstep — 18 decimal digits at the ceiling — and the gate proves it on the boundary value.

receipt-key-object-key.description: Reserved for the receipt-key record type (schema pending; plan Section 7.5): tenant and the receipt key ID, the SHA-256 of the encoded public key. Must stay in agreement with the receipt-key certificate's documented `objectKey` in `schemas/v1/ingest-receipt.json` — that flat certificate definition is what the receipt-key record type will consume, not duplicate (docs/notes/wire-schemas.md, open questions); tools/check-control-schemas.py cross-checks the two. An immutable record per key ID: rotation writes a new key object, it never rewrites an old one.
